opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The reason I think about it as a pyramid is that no single data source is enough on its own. Each layer gives you something the others can't, and they trade off scale against relevance to the robot.

At the very bottom you have the largest layer: internet-scale data. Text, images, videos of people doing things. None of it is robot data, but it's where a model learns common sense: what a cup is, that you open a drawer before putting something in it, what "tidy up the table" means. That's why building on top of large vision-language models has been so powerful. You inherit a huge amount of world knowledge for free.

In the middle you have things like simulation and human videos, especially egocentric video of people using their hands. Simulation can be scaled up cheaply and lets you explore situations that would be dangerous or expensive in the real world. Human video shows how physical tasks are actually done, in a huge variety of environments. But there's a gap. Simulation physics isn't perfect, and human hands aren't robot grippers, so you can't use this data directly. You have to bridge the embodiment gap.

At the top you have real robot data, usually from teleoperation. It's the most valuable because it's exactly the right embodiment, the right sensors, the right action space. But it's also the most expensive and slowest to collect. You need people, hardware, and time, and you'll never get internet scale from it.

So the pyramid matters because if you rely only on the top, you get a model that's very precise in a narrow domain but doesn't generalize. If you rely only on the bottom, you get a model that understands the world but can't actually move a gripper reliably. The magic happens when you combine them: the broad layers give you generalization and semantic understanding, and the small amount of high-quality robot data grounds that knowledge in real physical actions.

I'd also say the shape of the pyramid isn't fixed. A lot of the research frontier right now is about moving data up the pyramid, making simulation more realistic, or learning to transfer from human video more effectively, so that the cheaper layers become more useful. If we can do that, we can break the data bottleneck that has held robotics back for so long.

fable-5.1.text:
So when I talk about the data pyramid, I'm really describing a tradeoff between quantity and quality, and the key insight is that no single layer of it is sufficient on its own.

At the bottom you have the largest volume: internet-scale data, videos of humans doing things, text, images. There's an enormous amount of it, and it carries a lot of knowledge about the world, about objects, about how tasks are structured. But it's not robot data. There's no action label, the embodiment is wrong, you can't directly imitate it. So it gives you breadth and common sense, but by itself it won't make a robot move.

The middle layer is simulation and synthetic data. Here you can generate as much as you want, you have perfect labels, you can randomize environments, and it's cheap compared to anything involving a physical robot. The weakness is the sim-to-real gap. The physics are approximate, the visuals are approximate, contact is hard to model. If you train only in simulation, the policy learns things that don't quite hold in the real world.

At the top you have real robot data, teleoperation, real-world deployment. This is the most faithful signal, it reflects actual physics and actual sensors, but it's expensive and slow to collect. You're never going to get internet-scale real robot data. Even the largest efforts today are tiny compared to what language models are trained on.

So why does the whole pyramid matter? Because each layer compensates for the weaknesses of the others. Web data gives the model semantic understanding and generalization it would never get from a few thousand hours of teleop. Simulation gives it diversity and lets you cover the long tail of situations that are too rare or too dangerous to collect in reality. And real data grounds everything, closes the gap, and tells the model what the world actually feels like.

If you only build the top of the pyramid, you get a model that's good at the exact tasks you collected but brittle outside them. If you only build the bottom, you get something that knows a lot but can't act. The interesting research question, and honestly the thing I think will define the next few years, is how to connect the layers, how to make knowledge flow from the cheap, abundant data at the bottom up into the behaviors you care about at the top. That's why I think you have to take the entire pyramid seriously rather than betting on one source.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that different types of data solve different parts of the problem. At the bottom of the pyramid, you have large amounts of broadly available data, like images and videos from the internet. That can help a model understand the world—what objects are, what situations look like—but it doesn’t directly teach a robot how to act.

Then you have simulation data, where a robot can practice at scale, and real robot data, which captures the actual physics, sensor noise, and consequences of its actions. As you move up the pyramid, the data becomes more directly relevant to the task, but it’s also more expensive to collect.

So the challenge is to combine those strengths. You want broad knowledge from abundant data, lots of practice from simulation, and grounding from real-world experience. If you rely only on the top of the pyramid, scaling is very expensive. If you rely only on the bottom, you’re missing the connection between understanding something and physically doing it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that different kinds of data give you different things. At the top of the pyramid, you have real robot experience. That’s directly relevant to the task, but it’s expensive and slow to collect. Below that, you have things like simulation and human demonstrations, which can give you much broader coverage. And at the base, you have large amounts of images, video, and text that can help a model understand the world.

You need the entire pyramid because no single source solves the whole problem. Internet video can show you what a successful action looks like, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you what forces to apply. Simulation lets you practice at scale, but it doesn’t perfectly match reality. Real robot data grounds those capabilities in the physical world.

So the challenge is to make these sources work together: learn broadly from abundant data, then use robot experience to turn that knowledge into reliable actions.
